directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; bitter kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to the humid rainforests of West and Central Africa, this understory to mid-canopy tree bears a fruit whose bitter, astringent seeds are widely chewed fresh across West Africa, valued both as a traditional stimulant, similar in cultural role to true kola nut, and as an important item in traditional hospitality and ceremony. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and require the warm, humid, shaded forest conditions of their native range to thrive, making this a specialty planting for tropical botanical collections, ethnobotanical gardens, or large frost-free properties rather than a typical home garden tree. Water regularly, especially while young, and protect from any exposure to direct hot afternoon sun, which the shade-adapted seedlings do not tolerate well.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; kola nut is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. This West African rainforest tree bears large, star-shaped pods containing caffeine-rich seeds that are chewed fresh across much of West Africa as a stimulant and used ceremonially to welcome guests, and were historically the original flavoring source for early cola soft drinks before synthetic flavorings largely replaced them. Trees take many years to reach bearing age and need consistently warm, humid, partly shaded conditions similar to their native rainforest understory habitat, limiting cultivation outside the tropics to botanical collections and large frost-free properties. Water regularly, especially while young, and provide the dappled shade of taller companion trees where possible to mimic natural forest conditions.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gbanja kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; Gbanja kola is a frost-tender rainforest tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. The more widely commercially cultivated of the two main kola species, this West African rainforest tree produces large pods of caffeine-rich seeds that are the primary source of kola nuts in international trade, chewed fresh as a stimulant and once used as a flavoring base for early cola beverages before synthetic flavorings took over. Like its relative Cola acuminata, it requires many years of warm, humid, partly shaded growing conditions to reach bearing age, restricting realistic cultivation outside the tropics to specialty botanical or ethnobotanical plantings. Water regularly, especially during establishment, and provide filtered shade to replicate the tree's native rainforest understory habitat.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse.

directions: Plant seedlings in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Aidan fruit tree is a frost-tender West African tree realistic outdoors only in zones 10-11, elsewhere requiring a large heated greenhouse. Native to West African forests, this legume tree bears distinctive long, dark brown, four-winged (tetrapterous) pods filled with an intensely aromatic pulp used as a seasoning in soups and stews across Ghana and Nigeria, known as prekese, and long valued in traditional medicine for its aromatic properties. A member of the pea family, it fixes nitrogen in the soil like many of its legume relatives, and its distinctive winged seed pods make it an interesting specimen tree for a tropical botanical or ethnobotanical planting in frost-free climates. Water regularly while young, and expect pods to be harvested for seasoning once the tree reaches bearing maturity after several years.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; black fonio thrives on poor, marginal soils and needs no fertilizer, but requires consistently warm weather to mature its tiny grain.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; black fonio thrives on poor, marginal soils and needs no fertilizer, but requires consistently warm weather to mature its tiny grain. A close relative of the more widely known white fonio, this ancient West African cereal grass produces tiny, nutrient-dense grains on slender seed heads, traditionally grown in Togo, Benin, and Nigeria on poor soils where few other grain crops perform well, and prized for a quick cooking time and fine, couscous-like texture once hulled. It is one of the most drought- and poor-soil-tolerant of all cultivated cereals, requiring essentially no soil amendment to produce a harvestable crop, though its very small seed size makes hand-processing and hulling labor-intensive at home scale. Hand-harvest seed heads once they dry and turn tan on the plant, and thresh and winnow to separate the tiny grains before cooking or storage.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Guinea millet thrives on poor, marginal soils and matures quickly, traditionally valued as a fast emergency crop during lean growing seasons.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Guinea millet thrives on poor, marginal soils and matures quickly, traditionally valued as a fast emergency crop during lean growing seasons. Grown across the West African savanna, this small-grained cereal grass produces edible seed on slender panicles in a remarkably short season, earning it the common name 'hungry rice' for its traditional role as a fast-maturing food source that could be harvested before other slower crops during periods of food scarcity. It tolerates poor, sandy soils and limited rainfall better than most cereal grains, making it valuable in marginal growing conditions where more demanding crops fail, though the small grain size means threshing and hulling by hand is labor-intensive. Hand-harvest seed heads once dry, and thresh and winnow to separate the small grains before cooking as a rice or couscous substitute.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
Slow Food International Ark of Taste

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; African wild calabash produces small, bitter, non-culinary fruit grown mainly for its ornamental or utilitarian gourd rather than eating fresh.

directions: Direct sow after last frost into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun near a sturdy trellis or fence for the vigorous climbing vines; African wild calabash produces small, bitter, non-culinary fruit grown mainly for its ornamental or utilitarian gourd rather than eating fresh. A wild relative of the cultivated bottle gourd, this vigorous, fast-climbing African vine bears small, round, hard-shelled fruit that, unlike the sweeter cultivated bottle gourd, is intensely bitter and not eaten fresh, but the dried, hollowed shell is used traditionally as a small container, rattle, or utensil much like other calabash gourds. Its vigorous growth and attractive white, evening-opening flowers make it a fast-covering vine for a trellis or fence in a frost-free warm-season garden, valued more for ornamental screening and traditional craft use of the dried gourds than as a food crop. Harvest fruit once the shell hardens and the vine begins to die back, then dry thoroughly before hollowing and using the shell.
sources: Purdue University Center for New Crops and Plants Products
